g8-2023-007.quote: Which mixture tastes saltier? Explain your reasoning.
g8-2023-007.why: Item gives Function A as the equation y = 5/4 x and Function B as a table and asks which has the greater rate of change. This Cool-down pairs a table (Mixture A) with an equation (Mixture B) and asks which is 'saltier' - i.e. which unit rate is greater - exactly the same comparison across exactly the same two representations.

g8-2023-034.quote: What is the value of the rate of change for each situation
g8-2023-034.why: Item compares the rate of change of a function given as a table with one given as a graph. Problem 1b/2b of this activity ask students to find and interpret 'the value of the rate of change' for two proportional relationships each given in a different representation and say which is greater.

g8-2024-044.quote: Who makes more money after working 12 hours? How much more do they make?
g8-2024-044.why: Item gives Dog A as a table and Dog B as a graph and asks for the difference in their speeds in feet per second. Problem 1a asks who earns more and 'how much more', with one relationship given as an equation and the other verbally, after building a graph or table - the same compare-then-subtract-the-rates move.

g8-2024-048.quote: How much more do they make? Explain your reasoning by creating a graph
g8-2024-048.why: Item gives Store A as y = 3.5x and Store B as a graph, asks for each unit rate and then how much more 9 yards costs at one store. Problem 1 of this activity gives one rate as an equation and one verbally, asks for the value of each rate of change, and then how much more one earns over a fixed amount of work.

g8-2025-032.quote: What is the value of the rate of change for each situation
g8-2025-032.why: Item gives Alex's cost as y = 15x and Taylor's as a graph and asks which membership has the lower cost per month. This activity has students find 'the value of the rate of change for each situation' where one relationship is an equation and the other is a different representation, and decide which is greater.

g8-2025-048.quote: What is the value of the rate of change for each situation
g8-2025-048.why: Item gives Kaley's sleep as a graph and Mark's as a table, both stated to be proportional, and asks who sleeps more per night with an explanation. Problem 2 of this activity has students graph a table alongside a second relationship and state the value of the rate of change for each.

g8-2026-002.quote: Who makes more money after working 12 hours? How much more do they make?
g8-2026-002.why: Item gives Store A as y = 1.50x and Store B as a graph and asks which store charges $0.75 more per pound. Problem 1a asks the same two-part question - which is greater, and by how much - for two proportional relationships given in different representations.

g8-2026-048.quote: Who makes more money after working 12 hours? How much more do they make?
g8-2026-048.why: Item gives Splash Zone as a table and Tube Time as a plotted set of points and asks the difference in cost for 8 friends, showing how the table and graph were used. Problem 1a is the same 'who is more, and how much more' comparison with the two relationships in unlike representations.

g8-2023-020.quote: Using what you know about similar triangles, find an equation for the line
g8-2023-020.why: Item asks which equation represents the line through the x-intercept (9,0) and the y-intercept (0,-5); all four choices share the constant -5, so the work is the slope between two given points. This activity is the one place the course hands students two points on a line and asks them to produce an equation for it, then asks what the slope of that line is. Caveat: IM writes it from slope triangles rather than in y = mx + b form.

g8-2023-033.lessonTitle: Using Linear Relations to Solve Problems
g8-2023-033.quote: Write an equation for each line on the graph.
g8-2023-033.why: Item shows one graphed line and asks which of four y = mx + b equations represents it. Step 3 of this activity puts several lines with different slopes and vertical intercepts on one grid and asks students to write an equation for each, which is the same read-the-slope-and-intercept-off-the-graph work.

g8-2024-009.quote: Find the slope of the line that passes through each pair of points.
g8-2024-009.why: Item asks for the slope of the line through (2,2) and (-1,-2). This Cool-down is literally that task for three pairs of points, including pairs with negative coordinates, and its lesson is where the two-point slope procedure is developed.

g8-2025-008.lessonTitle: Using Linear Relations to Solve Problems
g8-2025-008.quote: Write an equation for each line on the graph.
g8-2025-008.why: Item shows a line falling from y-intercept 3 to x-intercept 6 and asks for its equation. Step 3 of this activity asks students to write the equation of each of five graphed lines; the lesson narrative notes this is where lines with positive, negative and zero slopes appear on the same axes.

g8-2025-035.activity: Similar Triangles on the Same Line
g8-2025-035.quote: What do you notice about the last column in the table?
g8-2025-035.why: Item shows two students drawing different slope triangles on the same line, getting 2/3 and 4/6, and asks whether both are right. This activity has students compute (vertical side) / (horizontal side) for three different right triangles whose longest sides lie on the same line, get 0.75 every time, and explain why - the exact fact the item tests.

g8-2026-008.lessonTitle: Using Linear Relations to Solve Problems
g8-2026-008.quote: Write an equation for each line on the graph.
g8-2026-008.why: Item shows a line with y-intercept -3 through (2,-2) and (6,0) and asks which equation represents it. Step 3 of this activity is the same task - read each graphed line's slope and vertical intercept and write its equation - for five lines at once.

g8-2026-020.quote: Using what you know about similar triangles, find an equation for the line
g8-2026-020.why: Item asks which equation represents the line through (0,9) and (3,0); here both the slope (-3) and the intercept (9) discriminate among the choices. This activity gives students two points on a line and asks for an equation for it and for its slope. Caveat: the y = mx + b form the item uses is established in Unit 3 Lesson 8, not here.

g8-2024-036.quote: determine whether it has no solutions, exactly one solution, or is true for all
g8-2024-036.why: Item gives 2(3x + 1) = x + 1 + 5x and asks whether it has no, one, two, or infinitely many solutions. This activity is exactly that sort: students distribute and combine, then classify each equation as no solution, exactly one, or true for all x. Its items 4b and 4c have the same distribute-then-compare-coefficients shape.

g8-2025-030.quote: Complete each equation so that it is true for no values of x.
g8-2025-030.why: Item asks for which value of h the equation 8 - 12x = h(3x - 4) has no solutions. This activity has students fill a missing term into an equation so that it is true for no values of x (and, in part 1, for all values) - the same 'choose the coefficient that kills the solution' reasoning, run in the same direction.

g8-2026-012.quote: determine whether it has no solutions, exactly one solution, or is true for all
g8-2026-012.why: Item presents four equations of the form 2x + c = k(x - 1) and asks which has infinitely many solutions; the distractors include one-solution and no-solution cases, so all three categories must be told apart. This activity asks precisely for that three-way classification over grouped triples of near-identical equations.

g8-2026-036.quote: determine whether it has no solutions, exactly one solution, or is true for all
g8-2026-036.why: Item gives 2(4x + 5) = 5(2x + 1) - 2x, with answer choices naming no solution, two specific one-solution values, or infinitely many. This activity asks students to decide for each equation whether it has no solutions, exactly one, or infinitely many, and to solve it when there is one.

g8-2023-041.quote: taking turns describing a move, then writing an equivalent equation
g8-2023-041.why: Item asks for the value of x in -8 - 5x = 20. This activity is the unit's fluency-solving activity: students take turns naming a move and writing the resulting equivalent equation, with equations such as -6a - 7 = 4a - 2. Caveat: the item's equation has the variable on one side only, so it is easier than anything in the activity.

g8-2023-043.quote: solve equations individually and then compare differing, though accurate, solution paths
g8-2023-043.why: Item asks students to solve 24x + 33 = 3(5x + 21) - 9 and show their work. This activity's instruction is 'Solve these equations for x' over multi-step equations with a coefficient distributed over parentheses; Activity 1 of the same lesson is built around 14x - 2x + 3 = 3(5x + 9), which is the item's equation in all but the numbers.

g8-2024-005.quote: Choose 3 equations to solve. At least one should be from your
g8-2024-005.why: Item asks for x in (2/3)x - 7 = 5 - (3/5)x. This activity's bank is exactly this kind - fractional coefficients with the variable on both sides, e.g. A. -5/6(8 + 5b) = 75 + 5/3 b and G. 4/m - 3/4 = -9 + 4/8m - and students pick several to solve.

g8-2024-046.quote: Check Noah’s work. If it is not correct, describe what is wrong
g8-2024-046.why: Item asks for the x that makes 1/4(3x - 8) + 4 = 2(x - 4) true, with work shown. This Cool-down is Noah's attempt at 1/2(7x - 6) = 6x - 10 - the same fraction-times-parentheses on one side, linear expression on the other - and it is where the lesson tests that skill.

g8-2025-014.quote: build fluency solving equations with variables on each side
g8-2025-014.why: Item asks which value of x makes -6(x - 4) + 5x = -9x true: distribute a negative, combine like terms, collect variables on one side. That is this activity's stated goal, and its sample equation -6a - 7 = 4a - 2 has the same negative-coefficient, variables-on-both-sides shape.

g8-2025-045.quote: Check Noah’s work. If it is not correct, describe what is wrong
g8-2025-045.why: Item asks for the x making 2/3(3x + 9) = x - 4 true, with work shown. This Cool-down solves 1/2(7x - 6) = 6x - 10 - a fraction distributed over a binomial set equal to a linear expression - which is the identical solving task.

g8-2026-021.quote: taking turns describing a move, then writing an equivalent equation
g8-2026-021.why: Item asks for x in 3x - 2 = 7(x + 5): distribute, then collect variables on one side. This activity is where students build fluency doing exactly that, describing each move and writing the equivalent equation that results.

g8-2026-032.quote: Check Noah’s work. If it is not correct, describe what is wrong
g8-2026-032.why: Item asks what value of x makes 1/2(14 + 4x) = 5(x - 2) + 2 true. This Cool-down works 1/2(7x - 6) = 6x - 10, the same halved-binomial-on-the-left equation, and asks students to verify each step - the same solving competence the item scores.

g8-2023-015.activity: Exponent Rules With Bases Other than 10
g8-2023-015.quote: practice using exponent rules to analyze expressions and identify equivalent expressions
g8-2023-015.why: Item asks which of (2^-4)^-1, (2^4)^-1, (2^8)^-2, (2^-8)^-2 has the value 1/16 - a power raised to a negative power, base 2, then read as a fraction. This activity is where students screen lists of expressions with bases 5, 3, x and 8 for equivalence using the exponent rules; the sister Activity 1 in the same lesson is what establishes 2^-n = 1/2^n.

g8-2023-047.activity: Exponent Rules With Bases Other than 10
g8-2023-047.quote: decide which expressions are not equivalent to the original. Be prepared to explain
g8-2023-047.why: Item asks whether 5^7/5^3 and 5^6 x 5^-2 are equivalent, with an explanation citing properties of exponents and the simplest-form value. That is this activity's task verbatim: Lin's list starts from a power of 5 and students decide which entries are not equivalent to it and explain why.

g8-2024-027.quote: Mark each equation as true or false. What could you change about the false
g8-2024-027.why: Item asks which of 3^10/3^5, 3^15/3^3, 9^10/3^5 and 9^3/9^5 equals 3^5 - half the choices bait students into subtracting exponents across mismatched bases 9 and 3. This activity is built on exactly that: true/false judgements about whether exponents may be combined when the bases differ.

g8-2025-016.quote: For each expression, write at least 3 different equivalent expressions.
g8-2025-016.why: Item asks which of (3^6 x 3^4)/3^2, (3^2)^2 x 3, (3^3)^2 and 3^15/3^3 equals 3^5 - a single base with power-of-a-power, product and quotient rules all in play. This activity has students generate equivalent forms of a power of 3 using those same rules, and its narrative lists power-to-a-power and multi-rule forms as what to expect.

g8-2025-033.activity: What Happens With Zero and Negative Exponents?
g8-2025-033.quote: From the work you have done with negative exponents, how would you write
g8-2025-033.why: Item asks for the value of 2^5 x 10^0 x 3^-2, which needs the zero exponent and a negative exponent written as a fraction, on bases that are not 10. This activity does both: it asks the value of 2^0 and then asks students to write 5^-n and 3^-n as fractions.

g8-2026-003.quote: Andre was trying to write 7/7 with a single exponent and wrote
g8-2026-003.why: Item asks which expression equals 12^20/12^4, with distractors 1^5 and 1^16 that come from dividing the bases. This Cool-down is Andre's mis-application of the quotient rule to a quotient of powers of 7, which is where the lesson tests dividing powers with a base other than 10.

g8-2026-015.quote: exponents can be added (or subtracted) only when the powers being multiplied
g8-2026-015.why: Item asks which expression equals (5^2)(7^-2)(5^4); the distractors 25^6, 17^4 and 175^4 all come from combining the bases 5 and 7. This activity's whole point is that exponents combine only when the bases match, with problems such as 3^a x 5^b = 15^c marked false.

g8-2026-043.quote: An expression that uses multiple exponent rules at once
g8-2026-043.why: Item asks students to use properties of exponents to decide whether (16^5)^4 is greater than, less than, or equal to 16^8 x 16^12, and explain. Both sides reduce to 16^20 by power-of-a-power and the product rule - the combination this activity has students produce and compare for a single rational base.
